name: The Talmud
fw: CCSS RL/RI/RH / C3 / IL SS 9–12 / Teaching About Religion
fwnote: The course reads a tradition's texts as literature and as historical sources in a public school, so it cites the reading standards for the band (RL, RI, RH, WHST), C3 history for 6–8, Illinois SS.H 9–12, and one of the six principles in "A Teacher's Guide to Religion in the Public Schools" (First Amendment Center) that the AAR 2010 Guidelines build on; alignment is the course author's judgment, not a certification or an endorsement by any of these bodies.

1.t: A Very Big Book of Questions
1.bq: Why is the Talmud so big, and why is it full of questions?
std: Identify the main topic of an informational text and retell its key details.
Know and use text features, such as headings and a table of contents, to locate key facts.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
1.write: Why is the Talmud so big? Tell about the rule from Exodus 20:8 and the list in Mishnah Shabbat 7:2. Say what each one says. Then say how the rabbis used questions to work things out.

ch.t: What Is the Talmud?
ch.bq: What is inside the Talmud, and how do people read it?
ch.talk: Why do you think one set of books needs so many parts?
ch.story: The Longest Shelf in the Library

l.look: Which number is the biggest? Which is the smallest?
Who is first in the chain? Who comes next?
Why might a book start with a question instead of an answer?

l.t: Words in the Middle, Words Around
l.look: If you wanted the oldest words, where on the page would you look?
Why might learning with a friend help more than learning alone?
Why does it take so long to read one page a day?
Which way tells you whose idea it is? Try saying something your teacher said the second way.

ch.t: The Torah and Its Rules
ch.bq: Why does a rule from the Torah need so many questions?
ch.talk: Do you think coloring is work? What would make it work or not work?

l.look: How is a scroll different from the books in your classroom?
What does this rule ask people to do? What word is new to you?
Are there more Do rules or more Do not rules?
How many more work days are there than rest days?
Pick one kind of work from the list. Why might the rabbis have called it work?
What does this rule protect? Why might the rabbis have put it first?
Why would being shy make it hard to learn? Why would a bad temper make it hard to teach?

2.bq: What do the rabbis' stories teach about being kind, giving, and learning?
std: Retell stories with key details and show you understand their central message or lesson.
Retell stories, fables and folktales from different cultures and state the lesson or message they teach.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
2.write: Pick one story: Hillel on one foot (Shabbat 31a), Honi and the carob tree (Ta'anit 23a), or Akiva and the water (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 6). Draw or tell the story. Then say what Jewish tradition teaches from it.

ch.t: Hillel on One Foot
ch.bq: What did Hillel teach a man who could only stand on one foot?
ch.talk: Why do you think Hillel gave a short answer instead of a long one?

l.look: How can you tell when a teacher is being patient?
Can two people both be fair and still disagree? How?
Why do you think Shammai thought the question was silly?
Say Hillel's rule in your own words. What would it mean at recess?
What did Hillel say was worth more than money?
How is this verse like Hillel's rule? How is it different?

ch.t: Honi and the Carob Tree, Akiva and the Water
ch.bq: What can a tree and a drip of water teach about learning and giving?
ch.talk: Have you ever done something nice for a person you will never meet? What was it?

l.look: Who did the old man say planted trees for him?
Which two numbers are the same? Why do you think the story uses the same number twice?
How might Akiva have felt learning with little children? What might have helped him keep going?
What did Akiva decide when he saw the hole in the stone?
What is one thing you could do this week for someone who comes after you?
What do the two stories have in common? What is different?

3.bq: How do people learn the Talmud together, and who do its kindness rules help?
std: Take part in conversations with partners, following agreed rules for talking and listening.
Compare one's own point of view with the points of view of other people.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
3.write: Pick one kindness rule from this unit. Tell what the Torah or the Talmud says about it. Name where it comes from, like Genesis 18 or Bava Metzia. Then say who the rule helps and how you could do it.

ch.t: Two Voices, One Page
ch.bq: Why do people study the Talmud with a partner, out loud, instead of alone and quiet?
ch.talk: Maya and Leo did not agree. What did they do instead of fighting? Why did that help?

l.look: What do you see the partners doing? Why do you think they sit two by two?
The saying has three parts. Say them in your own words. Which one is about a chavruta?
The two houses disagreed. What does marrying each other's children show about them?
Two sides were called true. Only one side became the rule. How can both things be so?

s.t: How to Be a Good Partner

l.look: Why would being shy stop you from learning? What could a partner do to help?
Which partner would you want? Say what Partner B did that Partner A did not.

ch.t: Kindness Rules from the Rabbis
ch.bq: What kindness rules did the rabbis write down, and who does each rule help?
ch.talk: Why did the class say the owner has to tell the secret part of the mitten? What would go wrong without that rule?

l.look: The rabbis read a story about Abraham as a rule for everyone. What is the rule?
Abraham made a very big meal for three people. What does that tell you about how he treated guests?
This is old English. Say it in your own words. What does it tell a child to do?
Which kid followed the rabbis' rule about shame? What did that kid do to help?
The verse talks about an ox and a sheep. What else could the rule be about today?

l.t: A Share for Those in Need
l.look: Why do you think helping someone earn their own is the best step?
Pick three cards. Say who each rule helps, and how you could do it this week.

4.bq: How did the Oral Torah travel from memory to the Mishnah, and why did the rabbis write it down?
std: Ask questions about people and groups who shaped important historical changes and continuities.
Determine the main idea of a text, explain how details support it, and summarize.
Teaching About Religion · expose not impose
Introduce a range of religious views without imposing any particular one.
4.write: Why did the rabbis keep more than one answer to a question? Use Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 and Mishnah Sukkah 1:1, and one more passage from the unit if you like. Tell what each passage says, then explain how the rabbis of the Mishnah and today's readers understand keeping the losing side.

ch.t: Written Torah and Oral Torah
ch.bq: How did Jewish teachers pass on the explanations of the Torah before anyone wrote them down?
ch.talk: Have you ever passed a message down a line of people? What helped the message stay the same, and what changed it?

l.look: Why might reading a book aloud from a scroll feel different from reading it silently from a printed page?
Why do you think the text lists who received the teaching, one after another?
This verse is nine words long. Name two questions a person might ask before they could follow it.
What is the difference between reading words aloud and giving the sense of them?

l.t: The Men of the Great Assembly
l.look: Think of one rule at home or school and invent a fence that would help people keep it.
About how many years did the Second Temple stand? Show how you worked it out.

s.t: Who Believed in the Oral Torah?

l.look: Put each answer in your own words. What does each side think a person needs in order to keep the rule?
Pick one of Hillel's sayings. Tell what it asks a person to do.
The Torah says dwell in booths. Why do you think the Mishnah starts with how tall a booth may be?

ch.t: Judah the Prince Writes It Down
ch.bq: Why did the rabbis gather the Oral Torah into the Mishnah, and what does the Mishnah look like?
ch.talk: The rabbi could have asked the general for anything. Why do you think he asked for a school?

l.look: What is the teacher trying to give his student in place of the Temple?
Each request saves something. What does each one save?
About how many years passed between the Temple's fall and the Mishnah? What could be forgotten in that time?
Why might a person be tempted to treat a small rule less carefully than a big one?
Add the six numbers. Which order has the fewest tractates, and what is it about?
Count the answers in this one mishnah. Why do you think the text gives all of them instead of just one?

l.t: A Book That Asks for More
l.look: Why would a short, clear rule book lead to a much longer book of discussion?
This is said to witnesses before a trial for a person's life. Why would a court want witnesses to hear it first?
Pick one link and say what you learned about it in this unit. Which link would a historian want more evidence for?

5.t: The Gemara and the Two Talmuds
5.bq: How did the Mishnah grow into the Talmud, and how does one page hold so many voices?
std: Use text features and search tools, such as key words and labels, to locate information quickly.
Interpret diagrams, timelines and other visual information and explain how they add to the text.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
5.write: Why did the rabbis keep the whole argument on the page, and not just the answer? Use Bava Metzia 84a (Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish), Ta'anit 7a (learning from friends and students) and Bekhorot 49b (deciding between Rav and Shmuel). Say what each passage says, and how readers have used it.

ch.t: Babylon and the Land of Israel
ch.bq: How did rabbis in two faraway lands turn the short Mishnah into the long Talmud?
ch.talk: Why do you think the rabbis kept the whole argument on the page, and not just the final answer?

l.look: Which of the Gemara's three questions would you ask first, and why?
Why did Rabbi Yochanan miss being argued with? What did the objections do for him?
This psalm is about the first exiles, long before the Talmud. What does it tell you about how the Jews of Babylon remembered the Land of Israel?
Why might it help to have a rule for deciding between two teachers, instead of picking one teacher for everything?
What might it feel like to be a farmer in row twelve, asking a question in front of the great scholars?
About how many years passed between the Mishnah and the Babylonian Talmud? Which came first, the Jerusalem Talmud or the Babylonian?
Can you think of another book, team or place with a name that does not match exactly where it is from?
Why might a tradition want to name the people who "finished" a book, even if the book was shaped by many hands?
The Yerushalmi covers more tractates than the Bavli, yet the Bavli is much longer. How can both be true?

ch.t: A Page of Talmud
ch.bq: How can people all over the world open the same book to the same page on the same day?
ch.talk: Miriam and Eli read the same page but in different ways. What did each of them bring to it that the other did not?

l.look: For each citation, say the tractate, the leaf and the side. Which one is on the back of a leaf?
The Mishnah gives a rule. The Gemara asks why the rule is written this way. What does that tell you about how the Gemara reads?
Which person at the table would you want to ask a question, and what would you ask?
The Mishnah did not say "nightfall." How did Rashi get there? What did he add?
Find two rules at school or at home that seem to disagree. Can you find the difference between the cases that makes both rules make sense?
How many years passed between Rashi's death and the first complete printed Talmud? Between Venice and Vilna?
If you started Daf Yomi on your first day of fourth grade, about what grade would you be in when you finished the cycle?
Why might people want to celebrate finishing a book together, in a crowd, instead of quietly at home?
Why might a teacher learn the most from students? What do students do that teachers do not?

6.bq: What do the Talmud's stories teach about arguing well and treating people kindly?
std: Recount fables, folktales and myths from diverse cultures and explain the central message.
Describe a character's traits, motives and feelings and how the character's actions move the events.
Work out a story's theme from its details and summarize the text.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
6.write: What do the Talmud's stories teach about disagreeing kindly? Use Bava Metzia 59b (the oven of Akhnai), Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 (hurting with words) and Berakhot 10a (Beruriah and the psalm). Say what each passage says, and how readers have understood it.

ch.t: The Oven of Akhnai: "It Is Not in Heaven"
ch.bq: When wise people disagree, how did the rabbis decide who was right?
ch.talk: Rabbi Eliezer had wonders on his side. The rabbis still said no. Was that fair? What would you have done?

l.look: Who said the oven could become unclean, and who said it could not?
About how many years passed between the argument and the finished Talmud?

l.t: Why the Oven Has a Name
l.look: Why might the Gemara compare a long argument to a snake? Give one reason of your own.
What is the sages' reason for not accepting the tree as proof?
What might the leaning walls tell a reader about honoring two people who disagree?
In the Torah the verse says the teaching is near. How did Rabbi Joshua use it in the argument?
Why might a parent laugh with joy when a child wins an argument fairly?
What did Rabbi Akiva do to soften hard news? Think of a time you had to tell someone something hard.
Why do you think the Talmud placed the oven story right after this Mishnah?
Which reading do you find stronger? Point to one detail in the story that supports it.

ch.t: Rabbi Akiva, Rachel and Beruriah
ch.bq: What kind of people were the rabbis of the Talmud, and who helped them become wise?
ch.talk: Beruriah changed one word in how she read a verse. How did that change what Rabbi Meir prayed for?
ch.story: A Better Way to Read a Verse

l.look: What did Akiva learn from the stone? What is something you learned one small step at a time?
What does this small scene show about how Akiva and Rachel treated each other?
What did Rabbi Akiva mean when he said his learning was hers?
Which of these numbers sound like exact counts, and which sound like "very many"? Why?
Rabbi Akiva chose this verse. Ben Azzai chose Genesis 5:1. Which would you call the bigger rule, and why?
What did Rabbi Akiva mean by comparing Torah to water for a fish?
Who lived first, Hillel or Beruriah? About how many years apart?
How does the end of the verse help Beruriah's reading?
Was Beruriah being rude, funny, or teaching a lesson? What in the story makes you think so?
What might "for the sake of heaven" mean for a group that is arguing, like the rabbis in the oven story?
Why might the Talmud want readers to know what jobs its sages had?

7.t: Fair and Kind: Talmud in Everyday Life
7.bq: How do the Talmud's rules about everyday life try to be both fair and kind?
std: Examine where rules, laws and key constitutional provisions come from and what they are for.
Identify the core civic virtues and democratic principles that guide governments and communities.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
7.write: How does the Talmud try to be both fair and kind in everyday life? Pick two or three texts from this unit, such as Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1, Deuteronomy 24:15, Nedarim 40a or Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5. For each one, tell what the text says, whom the rule protects, and how the rabbis or later readers explained it.

ch.t: Lost and Found, Honest Weights, Fair Wages
ch.bq: How does the Talmud try to make everyday trades, finds and jobs fair for everyone?
ch.talk: Why might splitting the coat be fairer than letting the faster or stronger person keep it?

l.look: The three gates have the same number of chapters. What might that tell you about how they were once one book?
Why do you think the rabbis asked for a promise before the two people share the garment?
What two things does this verse say not to do, and what one thing does it say to do?
For each thing, say why it is in its group. Which ones would the Mishnah say to announce?
Which side would you argue for, and what is one reason the other side might give?
An ephah measures dry things and a hin measures liquids. Why might the verse name both?
Four out of 24 is one-sixth. If a fair price today is 12 dollars, how many extra dollars would be one-sixth?
Which one does the Gemara say is worse, and what reason does it give? Do you agree?
What reason does the verse give for paying the same day? Who is the verse worried about?
Which reading fits the man's question, 'Is that the law?' better? What clue in the story do you use?

ch.t: Tzedakah, Guests and Saving a Life
ch.bq: What do the rabbis of the Talmud say a person owes to the poor, the guest, the sick and the person in danger?
ch.talk: Why do you think the rabbis said to dig even when you are not sure someone is trapped?

l.look: The verse uses the words 'heart' and 'hand.' What is the difference between hardening a heart and shutting a hand?
Why might the rabbis set a top amount for giving, not only a least amount?
Why might helping someone find work rank above handing them money?
The Gemara says Abraham was resting after his circumcision. How does his age make his running to the guests more striking?
What did Rabbi Akiva actually do in the room? Why might such a small thing matter so much?
Name one act of kindness that uses your body, one for someone who is not poor, and one that honors someone who has died.
Shmuel read 'live by them' as 'and not die by them.' Is that what the words say, or is it a reading he adds? Explain.
The Mishnah says this to witnesses in a court. Why would judges want witnesses to hear it before they speak?
Which of the three cases is about pikuach nefesh, which is about returning a lost object, and which one could be both?

8.bq: How is a page of Talmud built, and how does its argument move from question to answer?
std: Describe how a text presents information, such as in order, by comparison or by cause.
Distinguish among fact, opinion and reasoned judgment in a text.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
8.write: Does the Talmud care more about the answer or about the argument? Cite two or three passages from this unit, such as Berakhot 2a, Eruvin 13b, Mishnah Eduyot 1:5 or Bava Metzia 22b. Explain what each passage says and how different readers have understood it.
rooms: How to read a sacred text — the room

ch.t: Mishnah, Gemara, Rashi, Tosafot: The Vilna Page
ch.bq: How does one printed page hold a conversation that lasted more than a thousand years?
ch.talk: Why might it matter that every printed Talmud keeps the same page numbers? Who is helped by that choice?

l.look: How could you tell, just from the way the two voices talk, which one is the older text and which is the commentary on it?
What kind of help does a comment like this give a reader? Why might a beginner need it more than an expert?
Which of the two readers would you want first when you are new to a page? Which one helps you see the Talmud as a whole?

l.t: The Small Print at the Edges
l.look: How many centuries separate the oldest layer of the page from the newest? What does that tell you about how the page grew?
Which part of the line is the older teaching being quoted, and which part is the Gemara talking about it? How can you tell?
Why might a tradition that values argument tell students to acquire a companion rather than to study alone?

s.t: From Manuscript to Print to Screen

l.look: Which milestone changed how many people could own a Talmud? Which changed who could read it?
What does the Vilna layout tell a reader about how the text is meant to be studied? What might the manuscript have told its reader?
Roughly how many years passed between the first complete English Talmud and a free online one? Who gains from each step?
Sort the four addresses into the two kinds. What clue in each one tells you which kind it is?

l.t: The Six Orders and Their Tractates
l.look: Which orders do you think the Babylonian Gemara covers most fully, and why might that be?
Why might the Mishnah require an oath before dividing the cloak? Whom does that rule protect?

ch.t: The Moves of the Gemara: Question, Proof, Objection, Answer
ch.bq: Why does the Talmud keep the whole argument instead of just writing down the answer?
ch.talk: Which part of the class's board would help most if a new question came up next year: the final answer or the argument? Why?

l.look: Label each step with one word: rule, question, proof, objection or answer. Which step do you think takes the most skill?
If the reason for the rule is "the owner can prove it by the mark," what should happen with the plain pencil? Explain your step.
The Gemara gives two different proofs for the same rule. Why might it keep both instead of choosing one?
State the kushya in one sentence. Then suggest one way someone could answer it.
How does splitting "while working" from "not working" help protect both the worker and the owner?
Which ending tells a future reader more about the question? Give one reason.
Write the kal va-chomer: "If ___, then how much more ___." Then name one way someone could object.
What is the shared phrase in Hillel's argument, and what does it let him carry from one law to the other?
About how many years separate the end of the tannaim from Abaye and Rava? Why does that gap make a baraita a strong proof?
According to the traditional pattern, whose view would usually decide each case? What might explain a pattern like that?
Why would students need a memory word for six exceptions instead of a list of every case Rava won?
According to this passage, why did Hillel's house win? What does that suggest about how the Gemara values the way people argue?

9.bq: How did the rabbis build a new center for Jewish life after the Temple fell?
std: Analyze how events and developments connect within their wider historical setting.
Sort historical events and developments as examples of change, continuity, or both.
Determine a source's central ideas and give an accurate summary free of prior opinions.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
9.write: How did the rabbis keep Jewish learning alive after the Temple fell? Cite two or three passages from this unit, such as Gittin 56b (Yochanan ben Zakkai and Yavneh), Bava Metzia 84a (Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish) or Bava Metzia 86a (Rav Ashi and Ravina). Explain what each passage says and how traditional and academic readers have read it.

ch.t: Second Temple to Yavneh
ch.bq: How did a people whose Temple was destroyed turn a small town of scholars into the seed of the Talmud?
ch.talk: Yochanan asked for a town of scholars, not for the Temple or the city. What do you think he believed that choice would protect?

l.look: Put the four powers in order: Greek kings, Maccabees, Rome, Herod under Rome. About how many years passed between the first and the last?
Why might finding many copies of Isaiah in one library tell us something about what that community valued?
The three questions pull in different directions: care for yourself, care for others, act now. How do they fit together?
What can a historian learn from Josephus that the Talmud does not give? What does the Talmud offer that a battle report does not?
Three requests: a school, a family, a healer. What does each one protect?
The verse was written centuries before the Temple fell. Why would a teacher after 70 CE reach for it?

s.t: Yavneh, Bar Kokhba and the Galilee

l.look: Why might a court need its ruling to stand even when a scholar shows it may be wrong? What is lost if it does? What is lost if it does not?
Two sages, one leader, two verdicts. Why might the editors keep Akiva's hope in the text after the revolt failed?

l.t: Usha, the Galilee and Judah the Prince
l.look: Six orders hold sixty-three tractates. What does that arrangement by subject let a student do that a list of teachers in order would not?

l.t: Reading the Sources Side by Side
l.look: For each item, say whether it mainly answers what happened or what it means. Which item would you trust most for a date, and which for a value?
What stayed the same between the two scenes? What replaced what? Who leads in each one?

ch.t: Tannaim and Amoraim: Academies, Empires and the Editors
ch.bq: How did teachers in two lands, under two empires, turn three centuries of argument into one Talmud?
ch.talk: Why might a teacher feel he had lost more than a friend when his argument partner died?

l.t: The Tannaim: Teachers of the Mishnah
l.look: Why might teachers who trusted memory more than books care so much about exact words?

l.t: The Amoraim: Teachers of the Gemara
l.look: About how many years did the Amoraim teach in Babylonia? Why do these dates all carry a "c."?
Why might a text about study treat giving credit as so important?
How might studying in each city shape the questions a rabbi faced?
How many years passed from Rav's return to Ravina's death? What does that tell you about how long the Gemara took?
If you found a teaching in both notebooks, how could the differences help you learn about the teachers who wrote them?
Why might a community living under a foreign king need a rule like this? What limits might readers set on it?
Why would a teacher prefer a partner who objects over one who agrees?
Why would the Talmud keep Abaye's side of hundreds of arguments if the law follows Rava?
Which student do you think had more time and room to study? What in the reading supports your answer?

l.t: Rav Ashi, Ravina and the Savoraim
l.look: The line sets two pairs side by side. What does it suggest about how the rabbis saw the Mishnah and the Talmud?
How long did the age of the Geonim last? Why would a letter written in 987 matter for dates centuries earlier?

10.t: Sugyot in Paraphrase I: Time and Damages
10.bq: How does the Talmud turn questions about time and harm into lessons about living with other people?
std: Determine a source's central ideas and give an accurate summary free of prior opinions.
Distinguish among fact, opinion and reasoned judgment in a text.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
10.write: What does the Talmud think a person owes to others? Choose two or three passages from this unit (for example Bava Kamma 1:1, Bava Metzia 2a, Bava Metzia 58b or 83a, Shabbat 21b). Explain what each says and how its readers have read it.

ch.t: Shabbat, the Shema and Hanukkah
ch.bq: Why does the Talmud begin by asking what time it is, and what does that first question show about how it thinks?
ch.talk: Why might a book about law and life begin with a question about time instead of a question about belief?
ch.story: The First Page Asks the Time

l.look: Three answers are given for the latest time. Which one gives a person the most time, and which the least?
Which words in this verse does the Gemara use to explain an evening and a morning Shema?
Which marker would be easiest for an ordinary person to check in a village with no clocks? Why might the Gemara want more than one?
Add the rows. Which two groups make up more than half of the list, and what does that say about the world the list came from?
This verse says to keep the day holy but does not list what to stop doing. Where does the Talmud say the list of thirty-nine comes from?
In each case, whose hand crossed the doorway? Why would the Mishnah care about the difference?
What does this account leave out that 1 Maccabees includes, and what does it include that 1 Maccabees does not?

l.t: Hillel and Shammai on the Lights
l.look: How many lights would the House of Shammai set out on each night? Do both schools use the same total number over eight nights?
Match each case to its placement: the doorway, the window, or the table. What single goal explains the first two, and what different goal explains the third?

l.t: The Sons Who Came Home Late
l.look: Rabban Gamliel says the Sages agree with him on the real limit. Then why would they teach a six-hour rule instead of a twelve-hour one?
Which comes first in this verse, evening or morning? How does the Gemara on Berakhot 2a use that order?
Label each line as question, proof, objection or answer. Then write one more objection a study partner might raise.

ch.t: The Ox, the Pit and the Fire: Damages and Neighbors
ch.bq: When one person harms another, what does the Talmud say they owe, and why does it care about more than money?
ch.talk: Why do you think the Talmud asks so many questions about a single open pit? Where in your neighborhood could a "pit" be waiting?

l.look: What do the ox, the pit, the grazing animal and the fire have in common, according to this mishnah?
Who has to pay in this verse, and what does the one who pays get to keep?
Who should pay for the fence? Why might the Mishnah say a court cannot make Maya pay, but she is still responsible in a deeper way?

l.t: The Innocent Ox and the Warned Ox
l.look: Which case pays only half? What is different about that case?
The Gemara reads this verse as a rule about money. What problems with a literal reading does it point to?
Match each part of the story to one of the five payments. Which one would a modern court be least likely to count?
Why does the person who claims only half get one quarter, not one half?

l.t: Lost Objects and Giving Up Hope
l.look: What do you think "you may not hide yourself" means for a finder?
Why might the Mishnah treat this as a real wrong, even though nothing was stolen? What could someone in the chat do instead?
The verse forbids two things before it gives the command to love. What are they, and why might they come first?
Was the judge fair to the owner? Give one reason for the owner's side and one for the porters' side.

11.t: Sugyot in Paraphrase II: Argument and Mercy
11.bq: How can people argue hard and still treat each other with mercy?
